title: The Empty Tomb and the Risen Lord
summary: Early on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open; Peter and the beloved disciple run to it and find the grave clothes lying there. The risen Jesus meets Mary in the garden, then appears to the disciples behind locked doors, breathes the Holy Spirit on them, and sends them out. A week later he meets the doubting Thomas, who confesses him as Lord and God, and John states the purpose of his book.
story: The body of Jesus was laid in a garden tomb as the Sabbath began (19:41-42). Now, on the first day of the week, the story that seemed ended begins again. The Gospel that opened with In the beginning shows a new beginning in a garden, with a new creation breathed into being. The chapter moves from absence to presence: an empty tomb, then a voice calling Mary by name, then Jesus standing among frightened disciples, then a skeptic invited to touch his wounds. It also moves from sight to faith, closing with a blessing on those who will believe without seeing, which is every later reader of the book. Chapter 21 will follow as an epilogue, but 20:30-31 is the Gospel's formal conclusion.
historical:
The resurrection of Jesus is the church's first-order confession, and the Gospels present it as an event in history, not as a symbol or a private experience. Several lines of evidence are widely recognized, including by many scholars who do not share Christian faith. The tomb was found empty: all four Gospels report it, and the earliest opponents of the church, according to Matthew 28:11-15, did not deny it but explained it as theft. Women were the first witnesses, which is unlikely to have been invented, since in that society women's testimony carried little weight in court and the detail was an embarrassment to be explained rather than a claim to be made. The disciples, who had fled and hidden behind locked doors, became public witnesses willing to suffer for their claim. And Paul, writing to the Corinthians around AD 55, passes on a summary of appearances that he had himself received, very likely within a few years of the events (1 Corinthians 15:3-8), naming Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, and himself.

Other explanations have been proposed: that the disciples stole the body, that the women went to the wrong tomb, that Jesus did not truly die, or that the appearances were grief visions or hallucinations. Christian scholars such as N. T. Wright (The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003) have argued at length that none of these accounts for both the empty tomb and the appearances together, or for the fact that first-century Jews, who expected a resurrection of all the righteous at the end of history, came to proclaim that one man had already been raised bodily. The Gospels themselves record doubt: Thomas refuses to believe on others' word, and the disciples did not expect this.
cultural:
Jewish tombs of the wealthy were often chambers cut into rock, with a low entrance closed by a stone, sometimes a disk rolled in a groove. One had to stoop to look in, as the disciples do. The linen cloths lying in place and the head cloth rolled up by itself suggest an orderly scene rather than a hurried theft, since robbers would hardly have unwrapped a body soaked in spices. Mary's address to Jesus, Rabboni, is an Aramaic form meaning my teacher, a warmer title than the ordinary rabbi.

Peace be with you was the everyday Jewish greeting (shalom), but on the lips of the risen Jesus, spoken to men who had abandoned him, it carries the full weight of reconciliation. Thomas's surname Didymus is the Greek for twin. His confession, “My Lord and my God!”, uses titles that the Greek Old Testament used for Israel's God, and some interpreters note that the emperor Domitian, later in the first century, was said to have been addressed with similar titles; if John wrote during that time, the confession would have had a sharp edge.
literary: The chapter is built in four scenes: the empty tomb (1-10), Mary and Jesus (11-18), the disciples on Easter evening (19-23), and Thomas a week later (24-29), followed by the statement of purpose (30-31). Each scene turns on seeing. The beloved disciple sees and believes; Mary sees but does not recognize until she hears her name; the disciples rejoice when they see the Lord; Thomas insists on seeing and is blessed less than those who believe without it. Recognition comes through personal address, not proof alone, echoing the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (10:3). The closing verses tell the reader what the signs of the whole book were for.

outline.t: Peter and the beloved disciple at the empty tomb
Jesus appears to the disciples and breathes the Spirit
Thomas: My Lord and my God

doctrines.note: The resurrection is bodily. The risen Jesus can be touched, bears the marks of the nails, and yet is changed, appearing among locked doors. The church confesses his bodily resurrection as the firstfruits and pattern of the resurrection of all who belong to him.

Thomas calls Jesus “My Lord and my God!” and Jesus accepts it. The Gospel that began by saying the Word was God ends its main narrative with a disciple saying so in worship. In the same chapter Jesus speaks of his Father and gives the Holy Spirit, so the three persons appear together in the Easter mission.

“As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” The church's mission is modeled on Jesus' own and empowered by the Spirit he gives. The authority to declare sins forgiven or not forgiven is tied to that mission of proclaiming the gospel.

John writes “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.” Faith is not wishful thinking but trust based on testimony, and Jesus blesses those who believe through the witness of others, as every later reader must.

words.note: Pisteuo, to believe or trust. John never uses the noun faith in his Gospel, only the verb, nearly a hundred times, as if faith is always something done. In this chapter the beloved disciple believes, Thomas refuses to believe and then believes, and the book's purpose is that the reader believe and have life. Believing in John means more than accepting facts; it means entrusting oneself to Jesus.

Emphusao, to breathe on or into. It appears only here in the New Testament. The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses it for God breathing life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and for breath entering the dry bones in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 37:9). The echo suggests a new creation: the risen Jesus gives his people the life of the Spirit.

Anistemi, to rise or stand up. In verse 9 it is the word for rising from the dead, which the disciples had not yet understood from Scripture. The same verb is used in Acts for Jesus' resurrection (for example Acts 2:24, 32). It describes the dead being raised to life, not merely surviving as a spirit.

christ: This chapter shows that the crucified Jesus is alive in the body, the same person with the same wounds, now raised beyond death. He calls Mary by name, gives peace to disciples who failed him, sends them as he was sent, and gives them the Spirit. He speaks of My Father and your Father, My God and your God, drawing his followers into his own relationship with the Father. Thomas's confession is the high point of the Gospel's teaching about who Jesus is: he is Lord and God. For the church this is the center of the faith; as Paul says elsewhere, if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). John sets the evidence of eyewitnesses in writing precisely so that people who were not there can believe and have life in his name.

hard.q: Jesus gives the Holy Spirit here (20:22), but Acts says the Spirit came at Pentecost. How do these fit together?
hard.a:
Christians have read the two accounts in several ways. One view sees John 20:22 as a real but partial giving of the Spirit, or a symbolic pledge acted out, with the full outpouring for public witness coming at Pentecost fifty days later. A second view holds that John and Luke describe the same gift from different angles: John, whose Gospel ties the Spirit's coming to Jesus' glorification on the cross and resurrection, places it at Easter, while Luke emphasizes its public, empowering arrival. A third view distinguishes the Spirit given for new life and forgiveness (John) from the Spirit given as power for mission (Acts).

What both writers agree on is that the Spirit is the gift of the risen and exalted Jesus, that he comes to send the church into the world, and that the church cannot bear witness without him. The question of exact timing is second-order, and readers across traditions hold the views above in good faith.

questions: Mary recognizes Jesus when he says her name. What does that suggest about how the risen Christ meets people?
Thomas wanted evidence, and Jesus met him with it. How do honesty about doubt and trust in testimony belong together in faith?
John says these things are written so that you may believe. When you weigh the witness of this chapter, what do you find most and least persuasive, and why?
